posts.title: Your local store. Someone else's exit strategy?
posts.caption:
Opinion: A business should be judged by how it serves customers and treats workers—not just the price its owners can sell it for.

That is the question behind this account: when investors buy a business, who benefits, who takes the risk, and what happens to the people who depend on it?

We will scrutinize private equity using documents, clear explanations and corrections when the evidence changes. An acquisition alone does not prove wrongdoing.

What industry should we examine first: housing, healthcare or everyday services?

#PrivateEquity #WorkersRights #ConsumerRights

posts.title: Buying a business with borrowed money: who carries the debt?
posts.caption:
A leveraged buyout uses borrowing to help finance an acquisition. The important follow-up question is where that debt sits and which business must service it. Deal structures differ.

Debt payments can compete with other uses of cash. That creates questions worth investigating—not proof that a particular acquisition caused layoffs, higher prices or worse service.

Before accepting an owner's success story, ask: how much debt was added, who is responsible for it, and what changed in investment, staffing and service?

Opinion: Customers and workers deserve answers alongside investors.

Save this checklist for the next buyout headline.

#PrivateEquity #FinancialLiteracy #ConsumerRights

posts.title: Different signs. The same owner?
posts.caption:
A different brand name does not always mean a different owner. A roll-up is a strategy of acquiring multiple businesses, often in the same sector.

The competition question is what those acquisitions do to customers' and workers' real alternatives. Common ownership is a reason to investigate; it is not by itself proof of an unlawful monopoly.

The DOJ and FTC's 2023 Merger Guidelines discuss examining a pattern or strategy of multiple acquisitions. Guidelines are an analytical framework, not a court finding about any particular company.

Opinion: If your local choices are shrinking, the ownership map deserves attention.

Share this with someone who likes to know who owns the brands they use.

#Competition #PrivateEquity #ConsumerRights

posts.title: Workers belong in the deal review.
posts.caption:
Merger debates should ask what a deal means for employees as well as customers.

The DOJ and FTC's 2023 Merger Guidelines include an analysis of mergers between competing buyers, including employers buying workers' labor. That is an analytical framework, not a finding that any particular deal harmed employees.

Opinion: A deal's success should include pay, staffing, working conditions and meaningful job alternatives—not only an investor return.

A useful before-and-after checklist: wages, benefits, hours, turnover and staffing. Check other explanations before attributing a change to ownership.

What would you add to that checklist? Please avoid sharing confidential information or naming individual coworkers.

#WorkersRights #Competition #PrivateEquity

posts.title: After the buyout isn't proof of because of the buyout.
posts.caption:
A price increase, closure or staffing cut after an acquisition deserves scrutiny. Timing alone does not establish the cause.

Here is the evidence checklist we want to use:
1. Confirm the owner and acquisition date.
2. Document what changed and when.
3. Read financial filings or other primary records.
4. Consider competing explanations.
5. Separate allegations, research findings and opinion.

Opinion: Criticism of private equity is stronger when it can survive a fact check.

Save this for your next research session. If we get something wrong, send the supporting source so we can correct it.

posts.title: A successful exit. A better business for whom?
posts.caption:
Opinion: An investor's successful exit is not the only scorecard that matters.

When an owner sells a business, we should also ask what happened to service quality, affordability, employee pay, business investment and customers' alternatives.

Sometimes those outcomes improve. Sometimes they do not. The point is to investigate the actual record rather than treat the sale price as the whole story.

Our position: ordinary customers and employees belong in the assessment of a buyout.

Which measure would you check first—and why?

posts.caption:

We are looking for a question we can investigate with records and reliable sources. A personal experience can be a useful lead; it is not enough on its own to establish who caused a problem.
